claims.text: Sequential cold rolling followed by spatially controlled partial annealing can produce a bimodal or gradient grain-size distribution in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Fine-grained regions in the proposed heterogeneous microstructure will retain high strength.
Coarse-grained regions will facilitate plastic flow.
Coarse-grained regions can activate additional deformation mechanisms such as twinning or dislocation slip.
Different grain-size regions will undergo strain partitioning.
During strain partitioning, fine-grained regions will sustain strength while coarse-grained regions accommodate greater plastic deformation.
Dislocation slip and mechanical twinning can contribute to plastic deformation and strain hardening under high-strain-rate loading.
A heterogeneous recrystallized/non-recrystallized microstructure can combine high strength with substantial elongation in a high-entropy alloy.
The gradient-processed alloy will have greater ductility, including improved uniform elongation, than a homogeneous-grain baseline.
The gradient-processed alloy will deform more uniformly than the homogeneous-grain baseline.
The ductility improvement will occur without a significant loss of yield strength or ultimate tensile strength.
The gradient-processed alloy will retain its impact-induced energy-release capability.
Refractory high-entropy alloys can combine high strength, dynamic plasticity, and substantial impact-induced chemical energy release.
The untreated homogeneous-grain refractory high-entropy alloy baseline has limited ductility and non-uniform deformation.
The proposed strength-ductility benefit will hold under high-strain-rate impact conditions.
Using an inert or controlled environment during processing will mitigate oxidation effects.
The proposed benefit requires processing thermal exposures that do not cause deleterious phase transformations compromising strength.
